%% ------------------------------------------------------------- 1. TITLE
\begin{frame}[plain]
\vfill
\begin{center}
{\color{myblue}\bfseries\large
Maximum Nullity of Cyclic Covers of Graphs:\\[0.25em]
A Monodromy Ceiling and the Zero Forcing Number\\[0.25em]
of Generalized Petersen Graphs\par}
\vspace{1.0em}
Category: Mathematics \qquad Project ID: \rule{3cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}
\vfill
\kb{\centering We determine $Z(P(n,k))$ for \key{every} $n$ when $k=2,3,4$,
and for all $n\ge\SettleFive$ when $k=5$ --- proving a conjecture posed in 2026
and correcting a published theorem that is false.}
\vfill
\end{frame}

%% ------------------------------------------------------- 2. INTRODUCTION
\begin{frame}{INTRODUCTION --- the question}
\key{Zero forcing.} A coloured vertex with exactly one uncoloured neighbour
forces it to colour; repeat. $Z(G)$ is the smallest starting set that colours
everything.

\key{Why it matters.} $M(G)$, the largest nullity of a symmetric matrix with
$G$'s zero pattern, satisfies $M(G)\le Z(G)$. So a \emph{matrix} of large
nullity is a \emph{lower} bound on $Z$.

\key{The question.} What is $Z(P(n,k))$?

\kb{\key{What was wrong.} Rashidi et al.\ (2020) proved $Z(P(n,k))\le2k+2$.
Their Theorem 3.6, claiming $Z(P(n,3))=8$ for $n\ge12$, is \key{false}:
Krishnan (2026) exhibits $Z(P(12,3))=7$. The flaw is a case analysis that never
excludes $7$-vertex sets.}
\end{frame}

%% -------------------------------------------------- 3. INTRODUCTION cont.
\begin{frame}{INTRODUCTION --- the gap}
The 2026 note states as \key{Conjecture 5} that $Z(P(n,3))=8$ for $n\ge13$, and
says what is missing:

\kb{\itshape ``the content is the lower bound $Z(P(n,3))\ge8$ for all $n\ge13$,
which we verified only for $n\le20$\,\dots\ We will not assert it from finite
computation, which would reproduce the gap this note corrects.''}

It closes: \emph{``Determining $Z(P(n,k))$ for general $k$ \dots\ remains open.''}

\key{So the gap is uniformity in $n$}, not more computation:
\begin{itemize}\setlength\itemsep{0.05em}
\item combinatorial bounds must exclude all subsets at once;
\item matrix bounds need one matrix per $n$ --- infinitely many.
\end{itemize}
Prior work treats circulants; $P(n,k)$ is a \emph{block} circulant, so it is
not covered.
\end{frame}

%% --------------------------------------------------------- 4. FRAMEWORK
\begin{frame}{FRAMEWORK}
\key{The graph.} $P(n,k)$: outer $u_i$, inner $v_i$, edges
$u_iu_{i+1}$, $u_iv_i$, $v_iv_{i+k}$ (mod $n$). Cubic, and $\rho(i)=i+1$ is an
automorphism --- a \key{cyclic cover} of a two-vertex voltage graph.

\key{The matrix class.} $\mathcal S(G)=\{A=A^{\!\top}:a_{ij}\ne0\iff ij\in E,\
i\ne j\}$, and $M(G)=\max\operatorname{null}A$ over it.

\key{Two facts.} $\;M(G)\le Z(G)\;$ and $\;Z(P(n,k))\le2k+2$.

\kb{\key{Goal.} Exhibit $A\in\mathcal S(P(n,k))$ with
$\operatorname{null}A=2k+2$. Then
$2k+2\le M\le Z\le2k+2$, so \key{$Z=M=2k+2$} --- an exact value, not a bound.}
\end{frame}

%% ------------------------------------------------- 5. FINDINGS 1: ceiling
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 1 --- an exact ceiling}
\begin{block}{Theorem 1 (reduction), $n\ge2k+3$}
Eliminating the inner coordinates turns $Ax=0$ into one linear recurrence of
order \key{exactly $2k+2$}, with monodromy $T$, and
$\operatorname{null}A=\dim\ker(T-I)\le2k+2$, equality iff $T=I$.
\end{block}
{\key{Proof sketch.} Substituting the inner equations leaves a nine-term
relation with extreme offsets $\pm(k+1)$, so the order is $2k+2$; cyclicity
makes the solution space $\ker(T-I)$.}

\kb{\key{The ceiling equals the target.} $2k+2$ is also the best known
\emph{upper} bound on $Z$. So the method \key{either settles $Z$ completely or
cannot settle it at all}.}
\end{frame}

%% --------------------------------------------- 6. FINDINGS 2: obstruction
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 2 --- an obstruction}
Singularity is governed by a \key{symbol}
$F(s)=(s+a)L_k(s)+\alpha s+\beta$, monic of degree $k+1$ in
$s=2\cos(2\pi m/n)$, with \key{exactly three} free parameters for every $k$:
three roots may be prescribed, no more. Realisability is $c^2=a\alpha-\beta$.

\begin{block}{Theorem 2 (antipodal obstruction)}
$c^2=0$ identically $\iff F=(s+a)(L_k+t)$. Since $L_k(-s)=(-1)^kL_k(s)$, for
\key{every even $k$} a symbol with roots $y,-y$ has $c^2=0$; for odd $k$ there
is no such obstruction.
\end{block}
{\key{Proof sketch.} $c^2$ vanishes identically exactly when $F$ factors
through $L_k$, and the parity identity turns an antipodal pair into that
factorisation.}
\end{frame}

%% ---------------------------------------- 7. FINDINGS 3: congruence wall
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 3 --- the congruence wall}
A rational symbol drags its whole Galois orbit onto the grid. Taking $F$ as a
product of minimal polynomials of $2\cos(2\pi/d)$ gives \key{exact integer}
certificates: $Z(P(n,4))=10$ for $60,70,90\mid n$ --- the first exact values
for $k\ge4$.

\begin{block}{Theorem 3 (the congruence wall)}
Every rotation-invariant certificate is confined to \key{one} divisibility
class, containing \key{at most one prime}; and $e_2=-k$ for every such symbol
with $k\ge3$.
\end{block}
\kb{\key{Proof sketch.} Grid roots must form full Galois orbits, forcing
$\operatorname{lcm}(D)\mid n$. So symmetry is not a shortcut but a
\key{barrier}: to reach all $n$ it must be broken.}
\end{frame}

%% ---------------------------------------------------- 8. FINDINGS 4: tiling
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 4 --- tiling}
Drop rotation invariance: $T=T_{n-1}\cdots T_0$, and we need $T=I$.

\key{Docking.} $T_i$ sees only $[i-k-1,i+k]$, so fixing $k+1$ weights at each
end of a tile makes its product independent of its neighbours: tiles
\key{compose}.

\begin{block}{Theorem 4 (tiling)}
If an identity tile exists for every length in $[L,2L)$, then
$Z(P(n,k))=M(P(n,k))=2k+2$ for \key{every} $n\ge L$.
\end{block}
{\key{Proof sketch.} Every $n\ge L$ is a sum of lengths from $[L,2L)$;
concatenating gives $T=I$. In fact $[L,2L)$ is only \emph{sufficient}: $n$ need
only be a \emph{sum} of certified lengths.}

\kb{\key{An all-$n$ theorem, reduced to finitely many finite problems.}}
\end{frame}

%% --------------------------------------------- 9. FINDINGS 5: certification
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 5 --- exact certification}
$T_{\text{tile}}=I$ is rational in the weights, so bounding it directly needs
interval matrix products. Avoided: by Theorem 1,
$T_{\text{tile}}=I\iff\operatorname{null}A_{\text{one tile}}=2k+2$, certified by
the \key{bilinear} system $A(w)K(X)=0$, whose affine Jacobian lets a
\key{Krawczyk contraction} need only three norms.

\key{And the arithmetic is exact.} The box centre is dyadic, $f$ and $J$ have
integer coefficients, and $Y$ is \emph{arbitrary} --- so rounding it to a
rational costs nothing. Balanced limb decomposition keeps the product exact at
BLAS speed.

\kb{All \key{\NtileAll} tiles pass, $\alpha\le\MaxAlpha$; each $\alpha<1$ is an
\key{exact integer comparison}, not an estimate.}
\end{frame}

%% ------------------------------------------------- 10. FINDINGS 6: results
\begin{frame}{FINDINGS 6 --- results}
\begin{center}\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}clccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & settled & $L$ & certified tiles & $\max\alpha$\\
\midrule
$2$ & every $n$               & ---          & closed form   & ---\\
$3$ & every $n$               & $\LvalThree$ & $\NtileThree$ & $3.2\times10^{-10}$\\
$4$ & every $n$               & $\LvalFour$  & $\NtileFour$  & $7.6\times10^{-10}$\\
$5$ & every $n\ge\SettleFive$ & $\LvalFive$  & $\NtileFive$  & $1.0\times10^{-9}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}\setlength\itemsep{0.05em}
\item $Z(P(n,3))=8$ for every $n\ge13$, and $13$ is optimal --- this
\key{proves Conjecture 5}.
\item $Z(P(n,2)),Z(P(n,3)),Z(P(n,4))$ determined for \key{every} $n$, the last
two for the first time. \key{No divisibility conditions; primes included.}
\end{itemize}
The $k=3$ sequence runs $6,6,6,8,7,7,8,8,\dots$ --- non-monotone, which is
how the published proof went wrong.
\end{frame}

%% ---------------------------------------------------------- 11. CONCLUSIONS
\begin{frame}{CONCLUSIONS}
\key{How this answers the question.} The ceiling makes the method exactly as
strong as the target; the congruence wall shows symmetry cannot reach all $n$;
tiling breaks it and supplies the \key{uniformity in $n$} the 2026 note
identified as missing.

\key{Limitations.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength\itemsep{0.05em}
\item $k\ge6$: no tiles. $k=5$: threshold $\SettleFive$ not optimal.
\item $M(P(n,4))$ open at $n=24,28$ --- there $Z=10$ but no certificate.
\item Whether $M=Z$ in general is open; the rank law is verified, not proved.
\end{itemize}

\key{Unexpected problems.} A restart budget too small condemned a length that
does solve, and a stalling search was twice mistaken for non-existence.
\end{frame}
